title: About Me
text:
I’m originally from a small-ish suburb west of Chicago called Downer’s Grove. I grew up there with my parents, younger sister, and two cats. My parents’ willingness to let me dig up the yard to plant flowers is probably why I’m getting a PhD in horticulture today.
I enjoy outdoor activities like tennis, hiking, and trying to keep a garden alive. When I am not outside, I like to crochet, embroider, and dabble in 3D modeling. I try to learn new hobbies whenever I can.
I look forward to a future career where I can continue to engage my love of plants, people, and problem-solving.



I am very lucky that I have had many opportunities to explore and engage with the scientific community, as well as community in general. During my undergraduate degree at the University of Alabama, I worked in two different labs. The first studied invasive Johnson grass, which gave me my first taste of plant genetics and scientific presentations. The second studied stream ecology, which gave me grocery money and a chance to look at neat bugs all day. Toward the end of my time at Alabama, I spent two summers interning at Syngenta. The first intership was at their corporate headquarters near Chicago, and the second was at a field trialing site in Iowa. Through those experiences, I realized I was interested in the fields of agriculture and plant breeding. I made connections with experienced breeders, who suggested I apply to graduate school at the University of Georgia.
During my master’s degree at the University of Georgia, I met so many amazing people and participated in several valuable experiences. I gained bioinformatics experience, traveled for conferences and built my presentation skills, and learned about plant breeding from some of the most successful people in the field.
I went to North Carolina State University for my PhD partly because the research going on there was interesting, and partly because the Raleigh area is known to be a hotspot of biotechnology research. Since coming here, I have enjoyed the city and the people, and my new research on ornamental plants has been exciting. I hope that, by the time I finish this degree, I will have accumulated skills and connections that will help me in a career that is fulfilling and engaging, and I can do my part to improve the systems of agriculture and horticulture that people around the world rely on.

title: Education
text:
BS, University of Alabama
I attended the University of Alabama from 2019 to 2023, graduating Summa Cum Laude with a BS in Biology and a minor in Blount/Liberal Arts.
I was part of the Blount Scholars Program, as well as vice president of the Outdoor Adventures Club and a member of the General Art Club.
In the Spring of 2022 I studied abroad at Maynooth University in Ireland.

McKain lab
I worked with a team of graduate and undergraduate students to collect samples, isolate DNA, and construct DNA libraries with the goal of understanding the mode of invasion of Johnson grass in the southeastern United States. A fellow undergraduate and I presented this poster at UA’s Undergraduate Research and Creative Activities conference.


Benstead lab
I worked with a PhD student to sort through freshwater stream samples and isolate macro invertebrates. The goal of the project was to determine the effect of stream warming on invertebrate populations and, by extension, freshwater ecosystems as a whole.

title: Education
text:
MS, University of Georgia
I studied at the University of Georgia from 2023 to 2025. There, I had the pleasure of being part of the Institute of Plant Breeding, Genetics and Genomics, where I pursued my master’s degree in the lab of Dr. Dario Chavez. During my time there, I was the recipent of the UGA Graduate School Master’s Fellow Award and the John Ingle Innovation in Plant Breeding Award.
I participated in several academic organizations at UGA. These included acting as a committee member to help plan the Boerma Plant Breeding for Excellence lecture, joining the Graduate Student Association as the Griffin Campus Delegate, and participating in the Student Leadership committee to plan events for students on campus.
I was also fortunate to attend conferences and symposia across the country. I won 1st place in the NAPB Annual Poster Competition, Masters Division, 1st Place in the First Annual Griffin Campus Poster Competition, MS Category, and 2nd Place in the Norman F. Childers MS Student Paper Competition at the Southern Region ASHS Annual Conference 2025, among others. Building my communication skills and ability to convey my research has been invaluable as I continue my academic journey.

Chavez lab
As a research assistant in the lab of Dr. Dario Chavez, my work focused primarily on understanding the population structure of peaches and other Prunus species. I did this through the use of molecular marker data, as well as historical pedigree data, and applied my analysis to our own peach breeding program as well as worldwide peach populations.
Peaches, Prunus persica, were originally domesticated in China thousands of years ago. The process of domestication created trees with superior fruit, at the cost of genetic diversity. While peaches have since been carried across the world, China remains the cradle of P. persica diversity, and therefore a source of novel traits and possible disease resistance. Adding Chinese peaches to our germplasm collection would strengthen US peach production, but it is difficult for scientists to travel to China to collect samples. Dr. Chavez believes that the next best source may be Australia, due to a gold rush in the 1800s which brought Chinese workers, who themselves carried seeds to this new country. Using Capture-Seq technology, we have genotyped 250 Prunus accessions from across the world. The SNP markers derived from this diverse pool have been used to evaluate population structure across continents, affirming that feral peach populations in Australia may represent genetic material distinct from what is present in Europe and North America. In the future, these populations may constitute a valuable source of genetic diversity which could bolster peach breeding and aid in the development of new, stronger, and more desirable varieties of peaches.

title: Education
text:
PhD, North Carolina State University
As of August 2025, I am currently pursuing a PhD in Horticulture at North Carolina State University. As a research assitant in the lab of Dr. Hsuan Chen, I am studying native ornamental plants and working on developing molecular markers that can assist in selection and breeding, as well as doing physiological studies of several native plants.
I have also served as a committee member to help plant the 8th Biennial NCSU Plant Breeding Club Symposium.

Chen Lab
I am still in the early stages of my PhD reseach, but the projects I am planning to work on are as follows:

Marker-trait association in Cercis canadensis (Eastern redbud) using SNP markers derived from a diverse Cercis panel. The goal is to identify markers associated with traits like flower color and leaf glossiness, then develop KASP primers and other tools for marker assisted selection.
FISH characterization of Cercis species. Using probes targeting the 5s and 5.8s rDNA regions, we plan to fluorescently label chromosomes from six different species in the genus Cercis. This will allow us to differentiate between species and between individual chromosomes, allowing us to make more informed breeding decisions.
GISH characterization of Cercis hybrids. Hybridization of the species C. canadensis and C. chinensis is of interest to our lab. C. canadensis contains many valuable ornamental traits, like variable flower color and weeping architecture, while C. chinensis is hardy, resistant to some diseases, and has a novel, shrubby structure. GISH analysis of several interspecific hybrids can allow us to track crossing-over and visualize the ratio of genetic material from each parent in F1 and BC1 offspring.
Native ornamental species breeding. Several species native it North Carolina, including Amelanchia species (serviceberry), have potential as ornamental plants. However, lack of genetic material, germination protocols, and established breeding strategies make these species recalcitrant to cultivar development. Collecting material, developing protocols, and conducting gamma and oryzalin treatments will help further the development of these species as native ornamentals.
Cercis species rooting capabilities. C. canadensis and C. chinensis are propagated commercially across the country. They are primarily propagated by grafting, which can be time consuming and labor intensive. C. canadensis is known to have a limited capacity for rooting from cuttings, although C. chinensis is more capable of rooting. The question is, can rooting ability be reliably conferred to interspecific hybrid offspring. By collecting phenotypic data on rooting ability, and using the SNP markers developed earlier for Cercis, we plan to conduct GWAS to identify markers associated with rooting ability.

title: Experience
text:
Lab Work
My PhD research is being conducted in ornamental plant breeding, especially Cercis (Redbud) species. My projects include marker-trait association for valuable ornamental traits, development of marker-assisted selection methods for ornamental species, cytological investigation of Cercis species and interspecific hybrids using FISH and GISH methods, and physiological studies of native ornamental plants. During my master’s degree, I studied population structure of peach (Prunus persica) and other prunus species by combining genomic data with historical pedigree records. In undergrad, I assisted in multiple labs, studying invasive grasses and stream ecology. Click here for full info on labs.

title: Experience
text:
Internships

NA R&D Stewardship Intern, Syngenta
As the North America Stewardship Intern in Downers Grove, IL, my assignment was the streamlining and standardization of stewardship documents across all North American locations. This involved learning the programs SmartSheet and LucidChart, which were used by Syngenta to create records of every employee who received on-the-job training. I spent the summer contacting site leads and visiting sites across the Midwest to learn how we could improve the current system and accommodate every employee, including seasonal workers. The internship culminated in a presentation of my results to Syngenta’s regional leaders and my fellow interns.


Seeds Operations Intern, Syngenta
During my time as the Seeds Operations Intern in Slater, IA, I learned about the more hands-on aspects of agricultural research. In corn and soybean fields I planted seed trials, led teams to take tissue samples and hand pollinate corn, and took notes on variety performance. Indoors, I organized germplasm for genetic analysis, prepared seed requested by breeders, and built trial field layouts. I enjoyed the opportunity to experience both the corporate and field sides of agricultural research.

title: Experience

Other Jobs
In the last ten years, I have been fortunate to work in many areas, refining my communication skills and reinforcing my ability to adapt to any given environment. I have worked as a camp counselor, laser tag crew member, warehouse employee, babysitter, farm contractor, and bug-picker. I look forward to the new and exciting experiences that I know the future will bring.
